Austria

Canadian statement on the proposed treaty for the reestablishment of an independent and democratic Austria.
On January 14 in a memorandum submitted to the special deputies for Germany of the council of foreign ministers, the Canadian government stated that its essential interest in the German settlement was that it should provide the basis for a lasting peace. At that time the Canadian government was not prepared to submit its views on the substance of the German problem, pending consideration by the special deputies of its proposals for a procedure which would permit Canada and the other allies to take an appropriate part in the preparation of the settlement. The Canadian government proposed that appropriate participation might be achieved through the association of the other allies with the deputies, through committees or otherwise, in the actual drafting of those sections of the settlement in which they were most directly concerned.
In communicating this statement to the deputies, the Canadian representative made known that its observations on proposed procedure for preparing the German settlement applied mutatis mutandis to those envisaged for the drawing up of the Austrian treaty. No assurance has been forthcoming from the special deputies that a more satisfactory method of preparing the settlements will be adopted and the Canadian government has therefore not considered it advisable to appear before them to express its interest in the substance of these questions.
In the ease of Germany, in order to give all practicable assistance to the special deputies, and without prejudice to any representations Canada might wish to make at a later date, a memorandum containing certain preliminary views on the German question was prepared and submitted to the chairman of the deputies for Germany.
For similar reasons and in order that the reestablishment of a free and democratic Austria may be accomplished as expeditiously as possible, the Canadian government now presents below certain of its general views on the Austrian treaty.
The intention of the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States of America, the Soviet Union, and France to see reestablished a free and independent Austria, which was stated in the Moscow declaration of November, 1943, and in the subsequent declaration at Algiers of the French committee of national liberation, is one which earns the full support of the people of Canada. On January 30 of last year the Canadian government noted with satisfaction the steps which had been taken in Austria and which had resulted in the reestablishment of an autonomous Austrian state and of an independent Austrian government. At that time Mr. Mackenzie King stated that the elections which had been held in Austria in November, 1945, and the consequent reorganization of the Austrian government in accordance with the wishes of the people, were a welcome restoration of the democratic practice of government by consent, in a country liberated from the German invader.
The Canadian government now wishes to see a satisfactory settlement concluded between Austria and all the allies at the earliest possible date. It is in the Canadian view of vital importance that this settlement be of a nature to contribute to a set of circumstances most likely to ensure a permanent European peace. With

this main principle in mind, Canada supports the recognition of a free and independent Austrian state within the boundaries it possessed before the anschluss was imposed by Germany. The Canadian government considers that formal recognition of the newly constituted Austria, by ratification of the proposed treaty, should be followed, at the earliest possible date, by the withdrawal of allied forces of occupation, and that the authority exercised by the allied commission for Austria should, upon entry into force of the treaty, be transferred to the Austrian government. Only when all allied forces have been withdrawn and full powers have been restored to the Austrian government will it be possible for the Austrians to act as a free people.
In order to ensure the continuance of Austria as an _ independent and democratic state, it is the opinion of the Canadian government that the treaty should provide that the Austrian government will abstain in the future from any action likely to impair the independent status of Austria, and that any future anschluss with Germany should be specifically prohibited. Canada does not, however, consider that the signatories to a treaty should be asked to secure the future integrity of Austria, but rather that any threat to Austrian independence should be dealt with by the united nations. If the four occupying powers, however, wish to go beyond this and themselves make such a guarantee it is a matter which would not concern the Canadian government.
Of importance to the well-being of the people of Austria, and as a guarantee of the permanence of democratic institutions there established, the treaty should provide for the continuance of the democratic system in Austria, for the guarantee of fundamental human rights, for the prohibition of anti-democratic organizations, and for the elimination of the last vestiges of nazi influence in Austria.
In making this submission the Canadian government assumes that an opportunity will be provided for Canada and the other allies to examine the draft treaty with Austria before it is put in final form by the council of foreign ministers for signature and ratification.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Therefore for the period from 1935 down to 1939 there was no accumulated profit to be divided among the farmers of Canada; there was no participation to pay. In 1940 a balance was made which showed a loss by the wheat board of over $60 million, and that loss of $60 million was made up by the government of Canada. It is suggested by some that we should go back to that plan, that we should have the wheat board operating again as it was then operating, that the government of Canada should assume responsibility for any losses and therefore assume responsibility for seeing that there would be at all times a floor price payable to the farmer no matter what the world price of wheat might be.
If we are correct in assuming, and I imagine we are, that the farmer needs at least $1.35 a bushel in order to make it possible for him to produce wheat in western Canada and to maintain himself and his family at a proper standard of living, then in order to raise the price of wheat from where it was in 1938-39 up to $1.35 per bushel it would have required, not the $60 million which was required on that occasion to raise wheat 18 cents, from 62 to 80 cents a bushel, but well over $200 million. That is the amount that would have had to be taken out of the treasury of Canada in order to make certain that $1.35 per bushel could be paid to the western farmers for their wheat.
Having had this experience, those of us who live in western Canada and have farmed there are of the opinion that if that is all we are going to have in Canada for the future, if the only kind of wheat board we are to have is one which can only take the wheat when we have losses, and1 therefore those losses are to be charged up to all the taxpayers of Canada, some day we shall have a parliament which, because of the enormous costs of that kind of scheme put upon the taxpayers, will vote that system out of existence. Why would it do so? At the time in question, and no matter what the situation might be now, that wheat was going to the wealthiest nations in the world. We in Canada were being asked to finance the sending of 61 cent wheat to countries much more able to buy wheat than we are. The people of Canada sent it to them at 61 cents when we were paying to each of our farmers 80 cents a bushel for that wheat -and if we gave a price anything like what the farmers believed was required we would have to pay three or four times that much out of the treasury to make that wheat available to the people of those countries. As we sit here today after fighting a long war, and as we see some of those countries experience

great difficulty in financing, I think we are too much inclined to take into consideration the circumstances which exist at present and to figure in our own way that these people are going to have great difficulty in returning themselves to conditions somewhat similar to those which prevailed within five or six years after the first great war. Having been over there two or three times since the last war ended, and having travelled over a considerable part of that countiy, I want to emphasize the fact here, as I have emphasized it outside the house, that there is no other place in the world where 400 million people can live on as high a standard as the 400 million people can live in the territory between Britain and the Russian line-and when I say that I compare it with all of North America. If we had 400 million people living on this continent they would find it most difficult to live on as high a standard as the 400 million people who live today in Europe. I admit that having gone through six years of war they are experiencing great difficulties, but there is no other equal area of agricultural lands which can feed as many people as can the little peninsula known as Europe, nor is there any similar area elsewhere as rich in mineral wealth beneath the land upon which industry <;an maintain a great population and live at the same standard as it can in Europe. I believe that in due course they will again reestablish themselves to the position where they can buy the food of this country and can pay for it- not only in Britain but in the other countries of Europe.
Having, that point of view, Mr. Speaker, I believe we are justified not only in doing what has been done but in going somewhat further. As I stated a moment ago, from 1935 down to 1943. the wheat board did not pay participation, but in September 1943 the government under the War Measures Act passed an order in council under which all wheat in Canada was placed under the control of the wheat board. The order in council declared that wheat was to be marketed by the wheat board and that from that time forth the wheat board was to purchase all the wheat from the original producer and see that it was distributed in accordance with the wishes of the government.
Immediately we took over the wheat and made it the property of the wheat board we were able to value it at the market price of that day, and because we did that we were able to pay participation on the crops of 1940, 1941 and 1942. Later we paid participation on the crop of 1943. But even under that system we are three years behind in pay-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
ing participation. We have not paid participation annually. We have not yet started to pay participation on the crop of 1944, and this is 1947. So I am suggesting to the house that it is not correct to say that we paid participation annually under the wheat board from 1935 to 1943, or that we paid it annually, although we paid it on an annual basis, from 1940 down to 1945.
With regard to the period from 1943 to 1946 and down to the present, when the wheat board took over the wheat in Canada they had a carryover of approximately 600 million bushels. Since 'that time we have grown three crops, the first one 284 million bushels, the second 416 million bushels, and the third 305 million bushels-and that is leaving out the crop we are now handling. Three full crops were handled by the board, and they amounted to over one billion bushels of wheat which provided some three-quarters of a billion bushels of wheat to be actually handled by the wheat board. So along with 600 million bushels of a carryover the wheat board handled the wheat which was produced and placed on the market from three very good crops in the period intervening.
What was the situation at the end of the 1945 crop year? Seventy million bushels of wheat were left in the elevators; therefore we entered upon 1946 with 70 million bushels, plus the 420 million bushels which were grown in 1946, to be handled by the wheat board. This answers I think the suggestion which has been made that there has been some difficulty in supplying as much wheat to anyone in 1946 as was supplied to countries prior to 1945. We had a carryover of 600 million bushels at the beginning of the 1943-44 crop year; then we grew three good crops, and much of that wheat was in elevators at the seaboard ready to be shipped as boats pulled in for it. So the distribution of the wheat to different parts of the world was much simpler then than it is this year, when we have a carryover of 70 million bushels, and a crop harvested under difficult circumstances, therefore moved in the first instance rather slowly to market, and then moved about on our railways, again under difficult circumstances with the heavy snowfall that we have had this winter -both east and west. But in spite of that fact, Mr. Speaker, as the house was told the other day we have delivered 72 million bushels out of the 160 million bushels that we agreed to deliver to Britain within twelve months.
Therefore I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) is quite justified in saying that the whole 160 million bushels will be delivered to Great Britain before the end of the year which we are passing through.
But what I wanted to emphasize more than anything else was that this board handling wheat is a government board with absolute authority over the wheat. It was able to move it from our elevators and farms in the quantity of 1,300 million bushels to the different countries in which it was required, and market it to advantage in order to assist the people of the world who are in need of food, and at the same time give reasonable returns to producers. It is important we should realize that this board did that very difficult task during that period of time.

Whether we agree with this or not, or with the way in which it has been brought about, we must face the fact that our great northern neighbour, Russia, is growing into the world's greatest nation in agricultural production and in industrial development, bringing millions of acres under wheat cultivation in Siberia, a land which is comparable wth our own western plains. I think it is about time that we sat up and took notice and with the least possible delay started to do all in our power to enter into friendly reciprocal trade relations with our neighbours both to the south and to the north of us.
Canada can play a great part in bringing about a one-world family. Atomic energy has brought men to the cross-roads in our civilization. It will be one-world or no civilization. This propaganda of prejudice, hate and ignorance of each other spells chaos to Canada.
I have in my hand a table showing the average price received for all grains in Saskatchewan from 1911 to 1946. In that long period of thirty-six years wheat reached the dollar mark only fourteen times, and once reached a low of thirty-five cents, which meant about nineteen cents a bushel to the farmer when all transportation and service charges were taken care of. This is a strong argument in itself for stabilized parity prices with other branches of Canadian industry. Canadian Wheat Board Act
In only one year in those thirteen did wheat reach the dollar mark, and let me point out that the price of SI.05 in 1937 was purely a manipulated price on the Winnipeg grain exchange. When it was definitely known in the fall of 1937 that seed would have to be bought over a large area to seed the 1938 crop, speculators got into the market and wheat went to S1.05-purely a gambler's market. Six months later, when there was less wheat in Canada, and before the 1938 crop ever reached the market, the price was back to 54 cents.
This experience and the devastating effect it had on the economy of Canada in the years between 1930 and 1942 should have taught us a lesson that we should never forget. It clearly showed that, as the agricultural economjr goes down, all else in Canada goes down with it.
The farmers of western Canada want an all-grain marketing board, under the control of parliament, the people's representatives- one large pool. Private traders cannot handle the job, nor can any other group within the nation.
Some may call this bureaucracy. I would sooner have a bureaucracy under a democratic parliament than a bureaucracy of private monopolistic institutions, with no responsibility except to their own shareholders and that largely by proxy.
I do not care what the export price of wheat will be. We must have in Canada a price for all grains that will give us a balanced Canadian economy and a stabilized parity price. The products of industry must compare in price with the products of agriculture. The low prices of wheat which I have just quoted and the great contribution which the wheat grower has shouldered in domestic prices to the Canadian consumer to the tune of
8100,000,000-these things must not be forgotten when the new order is being drafted.
I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) to explain to the house the grounds on which the government decided that the wheat grower should sell all Canadian consumed wheat at thirty cents a bushel under the export price. I have been asked that question in my constituency and I have not been able to answer it. I would ask the minister to answer it.
My second question is, on what ground did the government sell Canadian wheat to forty-two countries outside of the United Kingdom at SI.55 a bushel, which was around forty-five cents a bushel under world prices?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill, an act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, has been discussed from nearly every angle and viewpoint. It is not my intention to go over any of these arguments again or to make much in the way of additional statement. However, during the debate there were various matters raised to which I wish to reply at this time. I should like to emphasize once again that the purpose of the legislation now before the house in the form of amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act is intended to provide a period of stability for wheat producers until July 31, 1950. In my opinion this is what producers generally have been endeavouring to secure over the years. The policy being carried out by the government is even more important when it covers the early post-war period when conditions abroad are so uncertain. It was only a few years ago that the organized farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in convention in Ottawa, urged the government to set a price for wheat at SI Fort William, Port Arthur and Vancouver. We all know that conditions in many ways have changed definitely since that time. We know that the farmer, as well as the rest of us, is paying more for the things he requires as a consumer. But I think that ini this short time we have gone a long way to bring to the deserving producer of wheat, who is so important in the economy of Canada, a substantial measure of security.
I wish to correct the impression left by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) that the government is asking for any powers requiring producers to sell grains other than wheat to the board. Under this bill the board will be enabled, with the approval of the governor in council, to buy, sell and deal in grains other than wheat, and thus afford to producers of such grains an optional method of marketing them.
Last evening I was asked to clarify the position in regard to the new domestic price for wheat for feeding purposes. The position is that the price of wheat for feed purposes in Canada increased by 33i cents a bushel as a result of the decision taken by the government to increase the domestic price of wheat, effective on February 17, 1947. I would point out, however, that the subsidy of twenty-five cents a bushel on wheat for feeding purposes is still being paid and that the free freight policy in effect in recent years
Canadian Wheat Board Act

good crop this year, but that crop does not exceed more than about 420,000,000 bushels. Domestic requirements during those three years will be 420,000,000 bushels. The remainder for export or storage would be
930.000.	000 bushels. Grain in storage may be increased by 375,000,000 bushels. Allowing for grain in storage, at an estimated amount of
375.000.	000 bushels there is left a remainder for export of 555,000.000 bushels.
If therefore we stored 375,000,000 bushels we would have only 550,000,000 bushels for export over the three-year period, or an average of only 185,000,000 bushels per crop year.
If we consider our flour exports this would not give us even enough to fill the United Kingdom contract. Moreover it is very unlikely that we would produce three crops in a row averaging 450,000,000 bushels. I cite these assumptions to show that any restriction on marketings during the contract period is unnecessary.
I was asked some questions by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I am sorry I am not in a position to answer one question at this time. However the information is being prepared, and I shall be glad to have the answers given while we are in committee, if that is satisfactory.
Is that with respect to feed wheat?

Yes.
Before concluding, I would ask the indulgence of the house to allow me to make a brief statement regarding Mrs. A. Kelsey of Erickson, British Columbia, who last December became the world's first wheat queen. Only a modest amount of publicity has been given Mrs. Kelsey's accomplishment and her work has been given no official recognition, which I should like to do at this time.
Mrs. Kelsey is a modest lady; perhaps that explains as much as anything why her fine accomplishments have had so little notice.
Born in Worcester City, England, where she attended school, and later living in Newport, Monmouth, she left in September, 1911, and arrived in Regina, Saskatchewan. She was married in St. Paul's Church, Regina, Saskatchewan, on May 6, 1913, to Mr. Charles Kelsey who resided at Keddleston, Saskatchewan, about forty miles from Regina. Because her health was frail, her husband and she later moved to Erickson, British Columbia, where she has resided since.
I have seen several pictures of the Kelseys' fruit farm, and it is to the credit of the Kelseys that they have since not only continued their fruit growing but have concentrated on the growing of seed grain. Com-

mencing in December, 1931, she has exhibited field corn, and since 1932 she has exhibited wheat. In the years that have elapsed she has won forty-three awards in all, including twelve for wheat and twenty-two for corn.
To demonstrate that she has not become the world's wheat queen by any chance of circumstances, I should like to list her twelve wheat awards:
1932, 2nd for a sheaf, Marquis, Vancouver. 1934, 2nd for 18 pounds handpicked, Marquis, Victoria.
1936,	2nd for 18 pounds handpicked, Marquis, Vancouver.

Throughout these years of concentration toward earning the world's highest award for wheat, she has had very indifferent health and occasionally very bad health.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that all Canadians will join with me in paying tribute to a courageous woman who has brought credit not only to herself but to Canada.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.

I should like to say a few words on this section. First, I would commend the minister for his action now in having brought to the attention of the house and the country the noteworthy achievements of Mrs. Kelsey in winning the world's highest award on wheat. It shows just how persistent the ladies are.
Hear, hear.

She is to be complimented on that and on the honour she has brought to Canada.
I do not wish again to discuss the principles of the bill. They were thoroughly discussed in the debate on second reading, and our views

Canadian Wheat Board Act
in respect to them were ably expressed by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley). I want to point out to the committee that there are two important principles involved in this bill. The first is the principle of long-term agreements with importing countries for food. That is a new departure in connection with the supplying of the world's food requirements, something that has not been done at least in modern times. We in this group believe that this making of direct agreements between the governments of exporting and importing nations is a step in the right direction. We are not surprised that there is opposition to it. For instance, we are not surprised that the more conservative members of the Progressive Conservative party are alarmed at it. Naturally they are alarmed at any change.
This change is something for which organized agriculture in Canada has been asking for a long time. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe appeared to be very much alarmed at this. He speaks or pretends to speak for the farmers of Ontario, but that is not the expressed opinion of the organized farmers, either of Ontario or of Canada. They have expressed their opinions on this matter at their annual conventions for a considerable number of years. Their opinions have been that there should be orderly marketing of our agricultural products and that there should be agreements with importing nations on basic food products. I should like to quote the latest resolution, part of which was quoted by the minister a few minutes ago, passed by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, as reported in the Manitoba Cooperator for February. This convention, representative of agriculture right across Canada, went on record as saying:
The convention expressed confidence in the operation of the Canadian wheat board and the management under its present chairman, and requested that the C.F.A. seek to have the Canadian wheat board made a permanent organization and be extended to be the sole marketing agency for all commercial grain.
I shall deal with that a little later.
At the same time the delegates voiced strong opposition to the reopening of the Winnipeg futures market, commonly known as the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Where was that resolution from?
From the Canadian Federation of Agriculture meeting in Winnipeg the early part of this month.
Do they take in Ontario as well?

I am surprised that an hon. member from Ontario should ask that question.
Surely he should realize that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture represents the whole of Canada, and I assume Ontario is still in Canada.
The second principle involved in this bill follows naturally from the first. If the government of any country is to be able to carry out its commitments with other countries in connection with the orderly marketing of foodstuffs it must establish a marketing board to carry out those contracts. That is what this bill does; it continues the Canadian wheat board until 1950.
I believe the powers of that board should be extended to permit the control and marketing of all grain in the Dominion of Canada. That is the expressed wish of organized agriculture in this country. From my contacts with farmers right across this dominion I feel quite certain it is their desire that the board should operate on all grains. As a matter of fact I do not think the board can do an efficient job in the marketing of wheat, in the regulating of the amount coming forward to market and in the regulating of the amount available for export, unless it also controls coarse grains. I am convinced that, before bringing in this bill, the government should have made a statement to the house and to the country on their coarse grains policy. That should have been done so that we could have discussed more intelligently certain provisions in this bill.	_
If the board takes the right under the bill to regulate the marketing of coarse grains, along with that right should go some responsibility for the price of the grain to the farmer. We do not know whether it is the government's intention to remove ceilings entirely from coarse grains. We do not know the intentions of the government with regard to present prices of coarse grains. At the present time those prices are entirely out of line with the price of wheat as laid down in the wheat board act. Until there is an adjustment of that relationship, I think the farmers of this country will be in a precarious position with respect to the production of coarse grains. Before this bill goes any farther, I think the minister should give some indication to the committee of his intention with respect to coarse grains.
This bill is brought in to permit the carrying out of the provisions of the British wheat agreement. There has been considerable criticism of that agreement in this house. The Hon. Mr. Strachey, minister of food in Great Britain, sat in the gallery here and listened to some of the discussion the other day. He is reported in a press report to have said that he wished he could have brought
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the official opposition in Great Britain over to the gallery here in Canada and have them listen to the official opposition here. He said that they were following an entirely different line in Great Britain. There they were criticizing the government for making too lenient an agreement with Canada, while in Canada our official opposition are criticizing the government because they did not make a little tougher agreement. It seems to me that (he government, with this bill, has probably struck something of a fair medium between those two extremes.
I believe the price of SI .35 as indicated by the government to the farmer in 1945 was fair at that time, but conditions have changed since then. When that price was announced by the government it was understood by the farmers that the price ceiling policy was to be maintained. If it had been maintained I do not think there would have been any particularly strenuous objection to that price.
Since that time the cost of production of wheat in Canada has risen by between fifteen and twenty per cent. On the basis of that rise in the cost of production, which is a responsibility of the government, the government should be prepared at this time to increase the initial payment to $1.55 a bushel. I do not think that increase would be any more than the rise in the cost of production since 1945.
I agree with the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture that in all probability it would be unwise for the western farmer or any group in Canada to obtain, through special legislation, concessions which would have to be paid for out of consolidated revenue fund to the extent of millions of dollars. I think sooner or later that would react against the group, whether it was labour, whether it was a farm group, whether it was a manufacturing or any other group in Canada.
I do not think there would be any danger in increasing the initial price to $1.55 at this time. The government have already sold a considerable amount of wheat, both the 1945 and the 1946 crops, and the prices were considerably over the $1.35 initial payment. Furthermore, the prospect of the price of world wheat remaining high for a further period of one or two years is much better at the present time than it was in 1945.
What was the highest price ever asked of the minister by an organized agricultural body-$1.35, was it not?
I think the minister would agree that much higher prices have been asked by the different farm organizations in Canada.
The highest price asked officially by the federation was an initial payment of $1.25.
That was the floor price, based on farm costs at that time.
When was that? Within the last four or five months, was it not?
No, that was a considerable time ago, at the time the price was set.
Two days before the contract was signed last July.
Not much more than four or five months ago.
Very much less than a year ago.

The government did carry on negotiations over a considerable period with farm organizations with respect to this wheat agreement with Great Britain, and quite rightly so. I have no doubt that these organizations at that time agreed on an initial payment of $1.35, plus participation certificates. I think the price was based on costs at that time. But since then the government has gradually dropped its price control policy, with the result that costs have gone up, and the government must accept responsibility for that.
As I said before, I do not think an initial payment of $1.55 for the five years would involve the government in any large expenditures from consolidated revenue in view of the reserves that have already accumulated and are likely to go on accumulating in the next year on the wheat agreement, and in view also of the amount of wheat being sold to other countries outside the British wheat agreement.
The agreement has also been criticized as being bilateral. It is claimed that it will be a hindrance to the making of multilateral agreements. But after what the Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon and from other things that have been said before, I am quite sure that will not be the case. For many years organized agriculture in Canada, especially the wheat growers of western Canada, have been urging an international agreement on the marketing of wheat between the principal importing and exporting countries and over the last ten years active negotiations have been carried on toward that end. They have not been very successful so far, but I believe that this action by the government of the largest wheat exporting nation in the world in making an agreement with Great Britain, the largest importing nation, has not hindered but rather helped the making of

Canadian Wheat Board Act
multilateral agreements. I think the proof of that is to be seen in what is taking place today. We are much nearer an international agreement on wheat today than we ever were before in the history of those negotiations and, as I say, I think this wheat agreement with Britain will help and not hinder an international agreement. I am sure that this government intends to establish international agreements to the fullest possible extent. In my opinion the only guarantee of stability to the producers of wheat in Canada is an international agreement between the importing and exporting countries covering periods of years. The international agreement must then be carried out by marketing boards within the countries signing the agreement. I do not think you could ever carry out such an agreement with the Winnipeg grain exchange operating. It would be physically impossible to do it. There would be no stability if a speculative market entered into the picture. The only way in which such an international agreement could be carried out wrould be through marketing boards in the countries which are signatories to the agreement. I think that must be the ultimate aim in the marketing of our wheat.
I am very glad that the minister announced that the government -would be prepared to take all the wheat produced in the pool period, but I was not quite sure from his statement whether the government agrees to take all the wheat produced in 1949 or just that amount of the wheat which happens to be delivered by August 1, 1950. I hope the minister will clear up that point. If there should be a shortage of storage space in 1949-50 and a certain amount of the wheat is held back on the farm, will the board accept that 1949-50 crop after August 1? I think they should, and I should like the minister to clear that point up.
To carry out these agreements it would be necessary to store grain somewhere in the world in years of surplus production. I am convinced that the importing nations should accept some of the responsibility for providing that storage. They should be prepared to build storage space in their own countries or in the country from which they are importing so that they can bear their share of storing the surpluses which it may be necessary to implement these agreements fully.
We shall have to assume responsibility within Canada for providing storage space. I am convinced that part of the grain should be stored on the farm. We should not depend entirely on the storage facilities at the head of the lakes and in eastern Canada, but we should start now, under the wheat board, an
ever-normal granary programme so that in years of surplus production some of the wheat may be stored on the farms where it is produced. The common sense of that was amply demonstrated in the drought periods in western Canada when we had to haul wheat all the way back from the head of the lakes to certain areas in western Canada to be used for seed purposes.there. In an area like western Canada, where our climate is such that we cannot count on anywhere near the same amount of production from year to year, an ever-normal granary plan should be established and part of the grain should be stored permanently on the farms where it is produced.
The government should assume some responsibility in regard to the storage of that grain. They should establish a standard form of granary which would be necessary for a farmer to build on his farm if he wished to take advantage of the provision of storing grain on the farm. They should pay storage on the farm. Not only should they pay storage on the farm but they should make some advance to the farmer on the grain stored on his farm for future delivery. I am not going to argue as to what that advance should be. Personally I believe it should be at least fifty per cent of the value of the grain. Whatever may be decided, some advance should be made to the farmer when he takes the responsibility of carrying that grain. Some allowance should be made to him for storage of the grain on the farm.
It has always been the opinion of this group that there should be a parity price for our grain, not only for wheat but for other grains as well. Our recommendation has been that the value of the participation certificate which is issued on wheat on which the $1.35 is accepted, or in case the government should see fit to advance the initial payment to $1.55, should be paid and that the value of the participation certificate should be based on the cost of production or a parity price. That price should not be a fixed price; it should vary with the costs of the goods the farmer has to buy. If these costs increase, then the value of the participation certificate should increase. If it decreases then the value of the participation certificate should decrease with it. It should work both ways. I believe the farmer would be satisfied with an arrangement whereby he received at any given period his appproximate cost of production or parity price.
I know the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has strenuously objected to this on various occasions and said that it could not be worked out; that it was not possible to estab-
Canadian Wheat Board Act

lish it. But I am quite convinced that it can be established and that there should be set up in Canada a commission which would determine what is a reasonable division of our national income as between the manufacturer, the labourer and agriculture, and on the basis of the findings of such a commission and the total production of Canada we can arrive at some fair division of that income. At the present time it is decided by strikes on the part of labour and agriculture, by the manufacturers' associations and other organizations coming to Ottawa and behind the scenes interviewing the government and trying to get for themselves certain concessions. That is not a fair way in which these things should be decided. It is much more intelligent for us to come out into the open, to set up a body which would arrive at some intelligent decision based on statistics, based on all the facts which they would have before them as to what that relationship should be. If we did that I am sure that we would have greater production in this country, because you can only get greater production when you have satisfied labour and satisfied farmers. That was proven without doubt during the war.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

I ask it solely for information. I have heard this word "parity" used in many different ways. Would the hon. member mind defining what he means by "parity". I assure him the question is not asked critically. I am really asking for his definition.

So far as the farmer is concerned, "parity" means the relationship which the price he gets for his products bears to the cost of the goods which he has to buy, a fair relationship between the cost of the goods he has to buy and the cost of the things he has to sell.

Thank you.
I just wanted to get the meaning the hon. member had in mind.
Is $1.35 a parity price?
I do not know.
The hon. member should.
I do not think anybody else knows or can know until he has made the necessary investigation to find out.

Each year?

asked by the hon. member for Calgary West, and I hope my answer was reasonably intelligent to him.

Not at all.
You go ahead and speak for them.
They have intimated that in this house on many occasions.
One hon. member did that just last night.

Also, the hon. member for Melfort just made the statement that all the farmers in Canada wanted the wheat board to handle all their wheat and grain.
Mr. AA^RIGHT: No, I did not. I said that the federation of agriculture had stated that, and just in designated areas. I am not speaking for eastern Canada. In anything I said I had reference to the act and the act refers to "designated areas" in Canada.

It is the official mouthpiece of the farmers.
The organized farmers.

Quite. The record will show it.

what he is saying.

culture for quite some time and I hope I can still speak for a few farmers in my own constituency in Ontario. I know they would not agree with that statement. As far as the prairie members are concerned, the hon. member for Melfort did not appear to know just what a parity price was. If he believes that SI.35 is a parity price for wheat now, I think he is badly mistaken.
He did not say that.

The hon. member
should stick to his programme and we will stick to ours.

The hon. member for Melfort also made the statement that the price would be constantly fluctuating. What is the meaning of this wheat agreement, then, if they want the price to be constantly fluctuating? I really think he is arguing against himself in a good many ways.
The east has been sadly neglected in this debate so far. It is a western problem bo a great- extent, but not wholly. As far as the wheat board handling our grain- is concerned,
I would give the farmers of Canada credit for being able to do some of 'their own business, and I really believe that some of the farmers in Ontario would still like to handle their own grain where they please and when they please. I say also that if the farmers are given this challenge that they have to be spoon-fed by any government, regardless of politics, then I believe i-t is a challenge the farmers of Canada will accept; and through cooperation I believe they can do part of their own business at least.

I am: happy to support this bill mainly because it is a legislative form of giving added stability to agriculture. We have heard a great deal about how important agriculture is to this country, and how to achieve that stability. It has been the concern of this government for many years, has been the concern of organized agriculture throughout Canada-, and today it is probably of more concern than ever to all those connected with agriculture. The government started out, with

-that aim in mind, by consulting at great length with all the various agriculture organizations in Canada, and adopted the practice of referring from time to time to organized agriculture. During the war, as one way of achieving that stability, the government started by closing the grain exchange. Then the government undertook the marketing of wheat for the farmers. The Minister of Agriculture this afternoon in his reply to the leader of the opposition made some pretence of dealing with that question. He said that we in Canada were tying ourselves to Great Britain and that we adopted the policy that in this transitional period it was to our interests and in the interests of Great Britain for us to enter into an agreement with that country under the terms of which we would sell our wheat to Britain at less than the market price, in the hope that if, in the future, the world price dropped below the original price in the agreement the British government [DOT]would pay us a price in excess of the then prevailing world price by virtue of this agreement. ment. The reason for that is obvious. We are getting stability of a kind. We are getting stability for a period of five years, but that stability is based on an average world price. It should be increased by one-third. Because I think it should be increased one-third, the price of wheat should be increased by one-third. If wheat were increased by one-third it would bring it up to more than 81.70 a bushel. Estimating it another way I believe that the farmer should have an income of $4,000 at the present time. The average cash income for Saskatchewan farmers for the last three years is $428 million, with $365 million of that coming from field crops. Therefore, if you take the proportion that field crops is to cash income you find that the farmer must receive $3,419 for his field crops in order to get a total income of $4,000.
In Saskatchewan the average farmer has only 170 acres of land in crop each year. Too much has been said from time .to time about the big farmers in Saskatchewan. The average farmer is a small farmer with only 170 acres in crop. With 170 acres and an average yield of 15-6 bushels an acre, the average crop will be 2,652 bushels of wheat. In order to seed 170 acres of wheat, it would take at least a bushel and a quarter per acre, which makes a total of 213 bushels. The farmer then has 2,439 bushels of wheat to sell, for which he must obtain $3,419, if he is to enjoy a decent standard of living. I say this would mean a price of at least $1.60 a bushel.
Much has been said about what we think parity might be. This might be my definition of "parity" at the present time. In order to get the size of the income that I feel would give the farmer a decent standard of living, the price of wheat should be at least $1.60 a bushel.
What has that to do with parity? What is your definition?
I would say that parity is a price which would provide a sufficient income to give the average farmer a decent standard of living.

Parity with
